record.field: The seven sections, and what each one answers

div.p: The app opens on the dashboard. Everything else sits under seven sections, grouped by the question you are asking — not by which table the data lives in. What your role does not cover is not shown to you at all.

tr.td: What needs you today
Open a Case · Cases · Consultations · Conflict Register
Hearings · Deadlines
All Documents · Document Generation · Signatures
Engagements · Time Entries · Expenses · Success Fees · Client Trust
AI Requests
Case Setup · Judiciary · AI · Signing · Technical

div.p: Do not navigate by menu when you are working a file. Open the case and stay in it: hearings, deadlines, documents, time and invoices are all on the case itself, and the Next Step line at the top says what the file is waiting for.

record.field: Every tile opens exactly the list its number counted

div.p: The dashboard is not a report. Each tile is a piece of work waiting for someone, and clicking it opens precisely the records it counted — never a similar list you then have to filter.

ul.li: Work in Progress — your open cases, this week's hearings, deadlines already past, cases still waiting on a screening, and time you logged but never marked billable.
Team (supervisors) — screenings that came back blocked, cases with no lawyer on them, and the case load per lawyer.
Oversight (managers) — AI answers flagged for review, and the client trust accounts.
Billing (accounting) — work that is billable but not invoiced, approved expenses waiting, engagements never activated.

div.p: The switch at the top of Work in Progress decides whose work the numbers count. A supervisor or manager opens on the whole firm — that is the practice they are answerable for — and narrows to their own files with one click. A lawyer has no switch, because their permissions already answer that question.
Red is late or blocked. Amber is due this week or needs a decision. Green is money. If nothing is red, nothing is overdue.
Start the day on the dashboard and empty red first. An overdue statutory deadline is the one failure on this screen that cannot be recovered by working faster tomorrow.

record.field: The intake wizard, step by step, with a worked example

div.p: Use Matters > Open a Case, or the button at the top of the dashboard. The wizard asks for what a file cannot exist without, runs the conflict screening for you, and creates the engagement in the same pass.

ol.li: Client, case type, responsible lawyer. The type decides how the file is handled — litigation, execution, consultation or other.
Opponents and other parties. Enter them here. The screening reads exactly this list, so a party added later means a screening that has to run again.
Conflict preview. Shown inside the wizard before anything is saved.
Fee engagement. Hourly, fixed, milestones or a success fee — or none for now.

div.p: A construction company asks you to sue a supplier over a delayed delivery.

ul.li: Client: Al-Sahel Construction. Type: Litigation. Lawyer: you.
Opponent: Modern Supply Est. — with its commercial registration number, because that is the key that catches the same company entered twice under two spellings.
Engagement: Hourly, 800 SAR. Every time entry on this case will now price itself.

div.p: The screening comes back clear, the case is confirmed, and the file opens on LAW/2026/00123.

The case is created and left in Draft. It cannot be confirmed until a legal manager overrides the screening with a reason recorded in their name. That is the design: a blocked file is a decision for the firm, not a form to be argued with.

Enter the identity or registration number of every party, always. It is the difference between a screening that catches a conflict and one that misses it because a name was typed with a space in a different place.

record.field: Three match keys, and telling certainty from coincidence

div.p: Screening compares this case's parties against every confirmed and closed file in the firm — not only the files the lawyer running it can see. A screening limited to your own book is blind to the conflict it exists to catch: your colleague's client.

tr.td: Certainty. The same partner is on both files.
Two records, one person or company. Duplicate contacts are the normal state of any client list.
A question for a human: «محمد عبدالله» and «محمد عبد الله» normalise to the same name, and may or may not be the same man.

div.p: Every hit records which key found it, so a reviewer can weigh it instead of guessing.

Matters > Conflict Register lists every screening the firm has run: case, client, lawyer, how many matches, the strongest evidence, and when it last ran. It opens filtered on Blocked; clear that filter to see everything, or filter to Certain Matches when you want only the hits nobody needs to judge.

You open a case for a new client against Northern Trading. The screening blocks: Northern Trading is a former client of a colleague, matched on same ID / registration number even though the name was entered differently. The register shows the earlier case reference, so the manager can read that file before deciding.

ul.li: Re-run the screening whenever parties change — the system voids the old result, and a stale clearance is worse than none.
Write overrides for the next reader: "Former client, matter closed 2019, unrelated subject, client consent on file" — not "OK".
Review the register weekly. A blocked screening sitting untouched is a case that cannot be worked.

record.field: What the system computes, and what stays yours

div.p: A hearing carries its date, court, circuit and the lawyer attending. Confirming it does two things: it starts the reminder, and it makes the hearing visible to the client in the portal. A draft hearing is your planning and stays private.

After the hearing, write what happened — what the court decided or asked for, what was submitted, what it was adjourned to. Client reports, case briefs and handover notes are built from this field; a hearing without it is a calendar entry, not an event on the file.
Statutory periods are proposed from configurable rules, then the lawyer adopts the binding date and records where it came from. The system is assistive by design:

ul.li: It does not calculate suspended periods.
It does not calculate official holidays.
It says so on the field rather than letting you assume otherwise.

div.p: Judgment issued 12 Rajab. The rule proposes an appeal deadline 30 days out. You check the court's own notice, find the period runs from notification rather than issue, set the binding date accordingly and write the source in the field. The dashboard now counts it, and the reminder is raised against you.
Record the source of every binding date in the same sitting. Six months later, "why this date" is a question with real consequences, and the answer must be on the record, not in a memory.

record.field: Two independent switches decide what a client sees

div.p: A document moves Draft → In Review → Approved (or Rejected, and Archived when it is no longer live).

Two conditions, both required, checked every single time the portal is opened: the document is published to the portal and it is currently approved. Withdrawing approval hides it immediately even though it is still marked published — publishing checks approval when you publish, and files change afterwards.

Marking a document Restricted limits it to the people you name, inside the firm. It is a stronger statement than the case's Confidential flag, which is a handling instruction rather than an access rule.

You draft a memorandum, send it for review, and a colleague approves it. You publish it; the client downloads it from their portal that evening. A week later new facts arrive, you move the document back to review — and it disappears from the client's page at once, without you touching the publish flag.
Publish nothing before approval. The portal enforces this, but the habit matters: a client who has already read a draft cannot un-read it.

record.field: From a logged hour to a posted invoice, with the numbers

ol.li: Log time on the case: hours and what you did. The rate comes from the engagement automatically — a zero-rate entry is refused rather than invoiced at nothing.
Mark it billable. Draft time is yours; billable time is the firm's to invoice.
Approve expenses. An unapproved expense is never billable.
Create the invoice from the case. The wizard gathers everything billable and not yet invoiced.

div.p: On LAW/2026/00123 (hourly, 800 SAR):

ul.li: 6.5 hours drafting and hearings → 5,200 SAR
Court fee 1,000 SAR, approved → 1,000 SAR
One 2-hour entry still in draft → not included, and the wizard names it and says why

div.p: The invoice posts at 6,200 SAR plus VAT through the standard Saudi e-invoicing chain. The two draft hours stay waiting on the dashboard.
Each time entry, expense, milestone and success fee is linked to the invoice line that billed it. That link is what makes double billing impossible — not a report anyone has to read.
Log time the day you spend it, and mark billable in the same action unless you have a reason not to. The gap between "worked" and "billable" is where a practice's revenue quietly disappears.

record.field: Their money, held apart from yours, with a worked example

div.p: A retainer is not revenue. It posts to a segregated liability account — the firm owes it back until it is earned — and becomes income only when a posted invoice is deliberately settled against it.

tr.td: Increases what the firm owes the client.
A separate, explicit decision — never a side effect of creating the invoice.
Requires a reason and a reference.
Requires both a source and a destination case.

div.p: The client deposits 20,000 SAR against LAW/2026/00123. You invoice 6,200 SAR and apply the trust funds: the liability drops to 13,800 SAR and 6,200 SAR becomes revenue. At closing you refund the remaining 13,800 SAR with the bank reference recorded.

ul.li: The balance cannot go negative — not even under two withdrawals posted at the same moment.
A case cannot be closed while the client still has an unsettled balance.

div.p: Apply trust money only against a posted invoice the client has seen. Applying it earlier turns a client's money into the firm's on the strength of an internal draft.

record.field: The portal, and how to put something in front of a client

div.p: Clients open /my/legal-cases — in Arabic at /ar/my/legal-cases — and see their own accepted cases only.

ul.li: Confirmed hearings
Parties you marked Visible in portal
Documents that are published and approved
Their own posted invoices
The money held in trust for them

div.p: Draft or cancelled cases, internal notes, fee workings, hours and expense economics, staff assignments, another party's invoice. These are not merely left out of the template — the fields are refused to any browser that asks the server for them directly.

ol.li: A document: approve it, then publish it.
A party: tick Visible in portal on the party line.

div.p: Before a client meeting, open the portal as they see it. What the file contains and what the client has been shown are two different things, and only one of them is what they will ask about.

record.field: Ask the AI from the case
Eighteen ready tasks, what each shares, and how to run one

div.p: On any case, Ask the AI opens a wizard listing the tasks that fit that type of case. A task is a request written down once — which agent, which data, what to ask for, who the output is for — so the lawyer picks it instead of assembling it.

tr.td: Full report of the proceedings to date · Update after the hearing · What we need from you
Case brief with follow-up recommendations · Chronology · Risk and settlement assessment
The next hearing · Missing evidence · Deadline audit · Execution plan
Statement of claim · Reply · Appeal
A legal question · Summarise a document or judgment · Review a contract
Handover note · Closing report and lessons learned

ol.li: Open the case and click Ask the AI.
Pick the task. A briefing appears under it: what comes back, what it will share from the case by name, and which sensitive extras it can use.
If the task works on a document, choose it. If it needs your facts or question, write them.
Sensitive extras — party names, internal notes, the chatter, money — are never added on their own. One box adds them, and they are listed by name so you know what that means.
Build the request. You land on it assembled: the right agent, the data ticked, the instructions written, and the exact redacted payload in front of you.
Read the payload, give consent, redact and send. The governance is unchanged: the task only fills the form.

div.h4: What the agent can read from the file
div.p: Composite entries, each still one line of the whitelist, redacted and shown in the preview: the hearings log with what happened in each, the deadlines, the document list (titles only, and a restricted document only to someone allowed to open it), the stage history — and, marked sensitive, the parties, the chatter, the financial summary and the internal notes.

A litigation file with four hearings and an appeal deadline ahead. You choose Full report to the client. The briefing says it will share the case reference, Najiz number, type, court, circuit, city, the stage history, the hearings log, the deadlines and the document list — no party names and no money unless you tick the box. The payload shows the four hearings with their dates and what happened in each; a phone number that had been written into one hearing note appears as [REDACTED-PHONE]. You consent and send, and a structured report comes back — current position, chronology, where the case stands, the coming dates, what is needed from the client, a closing line — for you to review before it goes anywhere.

ul.li: Write what happened after every hearing, the same day. The client report is exactly as good as that field.
For the assessment and the drafting tasks, give the facts in full. What you do not write the agent does not know, and it will leave it as [to be completed].
Do not add the sensitive extras to a client-facing task without a reason; a report to the client does not need your internal notes.
A legal manager adds the firm's own tasks under Configuration > AI > AI Playbooks. A new task chooses an agent and data and writes its instructions, and cannot tick anything sensitive by default.

record.field: Using the AI, and checking it

div.h4: Start from the case, not from a blank form
div.p: On any case, Ask the AI offers the tasks a firm actually asks for — a full report to the client of the proceedings to date, a brief with follow-up recommendations, preparation for the next hearing, the missing evidence, a deadline audit, a draft pleading, a research question, a document summary, a handover note, a closing report. Pick one and the request is assembled for you: the right agent, the right data ticked, the instructions already written. Sensitive extras — party names, internal notes, money — are offered by name and never added on their own. A legal manager can add the firm's own tasks under Configuration > AI > AI Playbooks.

Every send passes a consent screen that shows the actual text going out, with explicit ticks for what is included. Nothing is sent because a default was left alone. Agents do not work at all until the firm approves them — a decision, not a setup step.

Answers cite articles of Saudi statutes from the indexed corpus. Each request is flagged when it cites a repealed statute or cites nothing at all. Review those from AI > AI Requests, filter Needs Review; the same count sits on the manager's dashboard.

You ask for a memorandum on a labour dispute. The answer cites three articles. One flag appears: a cited article belongs to a statute repealed in 2021. You open the corpus, find the article that replaced it, and correct the draft before it goes anywhere near a client.
Treat every answer as a sourced draft by a capable junior: read the cited article itself, not the sentence summarising it. An AI answer is not a legal opinion and the module never presents it as one.

record.field: Roles and what each one adds
One chain: staff, lawyer, supervisor, manager — plus accounting

tr.td: Their own files.
Their cases and their team's; logs their own time.
The whole firm's cases, the conflict register, the case load per lawyer.
Overrides a blocked screening with a reason; deletion; the audit log; configuration.
Engagements, expenses, invoicing, client trust.

div.p: Each level inherits the one below it. A manager is also a supervisor and an accountant.
div.h4: Deletion belongs to the manager alone
div.p: That includes a file's activities and log notes. Everyone can mark work done; only a manager can make a record cease to exist. Identity and registration numbers are likewise readable by managers only.
Give a new lawyer the Lawyer role and add them to case teams, rather than raising them to Supervisor so they can see one file. The team field exists for exactly that.

record.field: What to check daily, weekly and monthly

ul.li: Dashboard: clear anything red. Overdue deadlines first.
Log today's hours today, and mark them billable.
Confirm tomorrow's hearings so the client sees them and the reminder runs.
Conflict Register: no blocked screening left sitting.
Unassigned cases: every open file has a lawyer answerable for it.
Case load by lawyer: look for the person carrying twice the median.
Billable but not invoiced: bill it or find out why it is stuck.
Approved expenses waiting.
Draft engagements — work billed against an inactive engagement prices itself at nothing.
AI answers needing review.
Trust balances against closing cases; a case cannot close with money outstanding.
The audit log, on any file where something unusual happened.

record.field: What this system does not do
Stated plainly, so nobody relies on it by accident

ul.li: No automated Najiz integration. Najiz numbers, links and Hijri dates are structured manual references, entered by a person.
No calculation of suspended periods or official holidays. Proposed deadlines are assistive; the binding date is the lawyer's, recorded with its source.
No parallel tax engine. VAT and ZATCA clearance stay with l10n_sa and l10n_sa_edi.
An AI answer is not a legal opinion. It is a sourced draft that a lawyer must read against the cited articles.
The Confidential flag is a handling instruction, not an access rule. Access comes from the case team and from a document's Restricted flag.

div.p: Each of these is a deliberate boundary. A system that pretended otherwise would be more comfortable to demonstrate and more dangerous to practise on.
